newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protesting French bank workers extend occupation.
newsitem.headline: Protesting French bank workers extend occupation.

text.p: Angry employees of the Credit Foncier bank decided on Saturday to extend their occupation of the bank's Paris headquarters into a third day after talks broke down with Finance Minister Jean Arthuis.

The employees, who have been holding the bank governor and other top executives as hostages since Friday in protest at government plans to dismantle the institution, said both sides had agreed to new talks but no date or time was set.

"We are disappointed. We had been waiting for a sign that the government was willing to change its mind about dismantling the bank, which it did not give," union leader Michel Lamy told Reuters after the talks broke down.
Arthuis said the government remained open to other options should a buyer for the troubled bank turn up.
But for the time being, the plan to spin off the bank's housing loans business to property credit group Credit Immobilier and then wind down the rest was the only proposal on the table, he added.
The minister had abandoned weekend travel plans to meet the protestors. He had initially insisted talks could be held only if they brought the captive governor along with them.

But he backed down after bank staff squatting in the ornate building refused to let Jerome Meysonnier go unless the government first axed plans to break up the firm, which it rescued from collapse last year.
The workers are fighting a government rescue package the state deems unavoidable unless another buyer turns up.
The workers fear up to 900 job losses at the 145-year-old property lender, which currently has 3,300 employees.
Arthuis had earlier criticised the worker protest as counter-productive but Meysonnier seemed unperturbed by the occupation of his headquarters by about 100 employees.
"I find this to be a form of brutality which prevents us from going forward, which prevents us from building," Arthuis told France Inter radio on Saturday morning.
But Meysonnier, walking freely about the building and looking relaxed and in fresh clothes despite his night in the bank, reassured reporters that the protest was peaceful.
"The night went well. Everyone was on their best behaviour," he said. Police were not called.
Employees said Arthuis' remarks had only aggravated the situation and accused state-appointed Meysonnier and the government of trying to fix the bank's future without them.
"The bosses want to do the negotiating while treating us like less than nothing," complained a man who said he had done 35 years at the venerable bank and could not afford to be named.

The government, which has always appointed the private bank's management because of its role in issuing subsidised loans, intervened directly last year to bail out Credit Foncier following a 1995 loss of 10.8 billion francs ($2.0 billion).

Arthuis launched a preliminary takeover by a state bank and now wants to carry out the second stage of his plan -- spinning off the core business to Credit Immobilier and passing the rest to a state shell company set up to manage its bond loans.
A collapse could have been disastrous for French financial markets, where Credit Foncier was once the second largest issuer of bonds after the state.
Arthuis has insisted it would cost taxpayers up to five billion francs ($1 billion) to put Credit Foncier on its feet.
But unions accuse management of overloading the 1995 results with 13.6 billion francs of provisions for bad property loans to make a wind-down of Credit Foncier appear inevitable.
